t.6.51.1: Having heard the lament of that king of the rākṣasas, Kumbhakarṇa then spoke these words and laughed aloud.
t.6.51.3: Swiftly indeed has the fruit of your sinful deed come upon you, just as a fall into the hells comes upon one whose deeds are wicked.
t.6.51.2: The very danger that we foresaw long ago, when counsel was being decided, has now come upon you, since you did not devote yourself to what was beneficial.
t.6.51.4: At the very outset, great king, this undertaking was not thought through; out of mere pride in your own valor, its consequences were not considered.
t.6.51.5: He who, having attained sovereignty, does later the things that ought to be done first, and first the things that ought to be done later, does not know the difference between sound policy and folly.
t.6.51.6: Deeds that disregard the right place and time and are performed perversely come to ruin, just as oblations are defiled when offered among the impure.
t.6.51.7: He who perceives the fivefold application of the three kinds of undertakings, and acts only after reaching an agreement with his ministers, keeps to the proper path.
t.6.51.8: And the king who wishes to settle upon a course of action in accordance with traditional teaching understands his ministers through his intelligence and keeps watch over his friends.
t.6.51.10: A king, or one who is like a king, who, having heard what is best among these three, does not understand it, has gained nothing from all his learning.
t.6.51.9: O lord of the rākṣasas, a man pursues righteousness, wealth and pleasure, or all of them together, each at its proper time, or else again the three pairs.
t.6.51.12: He who, self-possessed, after taking counsel together with his ministers, pursues dharma, artha and kāma each at its proper time, will not meet with calamity in this world.
t.6.51.11: Gifts or conciliation, sowing dissension, and valor at the proper time, and their combined use, O best of rākṣasas, and also those two, sound policy and unsound policy.
t.6.51.14: Men of beast-like understanding, without having grasped the meaning of the treatises, wish out of sheer boldness to speak when they have been admitted into the inner circle of counsels.
t.6.51.13: A king who, together with ministers who know the true nature of affairs, examines what he should and should not do here for his own sake, with an eye to its beneficial consequences, lives on securely.
t.6.51.15: The harmful words of those who are unversed in the śāstras and ignorant of the science of statecraft, even though they desire great prosperity, should not be acted upon.
t.6.51.17: Here in this world, ministers who have joined with clever enemies bring ruin upon their master by making him undertake deeds that are wrong and contrary to his interest.
t.6.51.16: Those men who out of impudence speak what is harmful but wears the guise of what is beneficial should, after due scrutiny, be kept out of counsel, for they are spoilers of the undertaking.
t.6.51.18: When deciding on counsel, a master should recognize by their conduct those ministers gathered about him who, though they seem to be friends, are in truth enemies.
t.6.51.20: Indeed, he who, disregarding his enemy, does not guard himself meets with misfortunes and is cast down from his position.
t.6.51.19: Here in this world, others find a weak spot in the fickle man who rashly rushes after his undertakings, just as birds enter the opening in Krauñca.
t.6.51.21: But Daśagrīva, having heard those words of Kumbhakarṇa, knitted his brows in a frown, and in anger he spoke to him.
t.6.51.22: Why do you instruct me as though you were a venerable guru, a teacher? Why exert yourself with words like this? Let what is fitting for the time be done.
t.6.51.24: Whatever is fitting at this time, let that now be done. By your valour, set right the fault born of my bad conduct.
t.6.51.23: Whatever was not undertaken before, whether through error, delusion of mind, or reliance on strength and valor, do not now again raise useless words about it.
t.6.51.25: If indeed there is affection for me, or if you acknowledge our brotherhood, or if this task is held in your heart as the most urgent of all that must be done,
t.6.51.26: He is a true friend who comes to the aid of one who is wretched and whose fortunes are ruined; he is a true kinsman who stands ready to help when one has gone astray through misdeeds.
t.6.51.27: Then, as he spoke these words, steady yet harsh, the other, realizing that he was angry, spoke to him slowly and gently.
t.6.51.28: Seeing that his brother was deeply agitated in his senses, Kumbhakarṇa spoke these words slowly, consoling him.
t.6.51.30: Do not take this to heart, O king, while I am alive; I shall destroy him on whose account you are tormented.
t.6.51.29: Enough, O lord of the kings of the rākṣasas, of falling into this anguish of yours! Casting off your anger as well, you ought to regain your composure.
t.6.51.31: What is beneficial must certainly be told to you by me in every circumstance; it has been spoken out of kinship and brotherly affection, O king.
t.6.51.32: Behold the slaughter of the enemies that I shall now work in battle, such as is fitting for an affectionate kinsman to do at this time.
t.6.51.33: Today, O mighty-armed one, behold the army of monkeys fleeing once Rāma, together with his brother, has been slain by me at the forefront of battle.
t.6.51.34: Today, mighty-armed one, when you have seen that head of Rāma brought by me from the battlefield, be happy, and let Sītā be filled with sorrow.
t.6.51.35: Today let all the rākṣasas in Laṅkā whose kinsmen have been slain behold the death of Rāma, a sight most great and pleasing.
t.6.51.36: Today, by destroying the enemy in battle, I shall wipe away the tears of those overwhelmed with grief because of the slaying of their own kinsmen.
t.6.51.37: Today, in battle, behold Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, who resembles a mountain, scattered like a cloud with the sun upon it.
t.6.51.38: No one else should be sent by you into battle, O you of unequalled prowess; I myself shall destroy your enemies, O mighty one.
t.6.51.39: Whether it be Śakra, or Yama, or Pāvaka and Māruta, I shall fight them all, and Kubera and Varuṇa too.
t.6.51.40: Even Puraṃdara would be afraid of me as I roar, my body the size of a mountain, bearing a sharp spear and with sharp fangs.
t.6.51.42: Not with a spear, nor with a mace, nor with a sword, nor with sharp arrows, but with my two hands alone, enraged, I shall slay even the wielder of the thunderbolt.
t.6.51.41: Or else, even when I have cast aside my weapons and advance with force to crush my foes, no one who wishes to live is able to stand before me.
t.6.51.43: If that Rāghava today withstands the force of my fist, then those floods of arrows shall drink the blood of Rāghava.
t.6.51.45: O king, cast off your fear of Rāma; here in battle I shall slay Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, and the mighty Sugrīva as well. I wish to bestow upon you great and unparalleled glory.
t.6.51.44: O king, why are you tormented by anxiety while I am here? I am ready to go forth to destroy your enemies.
t.6.51.46: Through the slaying of Dāśarathi I go to win for you a happiness that brings you joy; having killed Rāma together with Lakṣmaṇa, I shall devour all the foremost leaders of the monkey troops.
t.6.51.47: Enjoy yourself as you please, drink the finest liquor, attend to your affairs, and let your fever be dispelled; once Rāma has been sent by me today to the abode of Yama, Sītā will at long last come under your control.
